n: Having instructed the Twelve, Jesus continues his own preaching tour through the towns of Galilee.

f.w: when Jesus had made an end

n: John the Baptist is now in prison, arrested by Herod Antipas. Hearing reports about Jesus, he sends two of his disciples to him.

f.g: The historian Josephus places John’s imprisonment at Machaerus, a fortress east of the Dead Sea.

n: The question — “Are you the one who is to come?” — may have been asked for his disciples’ sake, or out of John’s own struggle in prison. Either way, it is honest.

f.g: A title for the expected Messiah.

n: Instead of a simple yes, Jesus invites them to report what they themselves have heard and seen.

f.g: shew = show, tell.

n: His works echo Isaiah’s prophecies of what the Messiah would do. John, who knew those scriptures well, would understand the answer.

f.w: the poor have the gospel preached to them

n: A gentle blessing: happy is the person who doesn’t stumble over Jesus because he isn’t the kind of Messiah they expected.

f.g: Greek skandalizō — to stumble or be tripped up.

n: Now Jesus praises John. Did the crowds go into the desert to see someone flimsy, swaying with every breeze like the reeds along the Jordan? Certainly not.

f.w: A reed shaken with the wind
f.g: Reeds grew along the Jordan; the image means a weak, wavering person.

n: John was no pampered courtier in fine clothes. He wore camel’s hair and lived in the wilderness.

f.g: raiment = clothing; soft = luxurious.

n: John was a prophet — and more than a prophet, because he personally prepared the way for, and baptized, the Messiah.
Jesus identifies John as the messenger Malachi foretold, sent ahead to prepare the Lord’s way.

f.w: I send my messenger before thy face

n: No one born of a woman was greater than John. Yet the least in God’s kingdom is greater still. Joseph Smith taught that “he that is least” refers to Jesus himself.

f.w: he that is least in the kingdom of heaven
f.g: Joseph Smith explained this as Jesus, who was considered least by people of his day.

n: A difficult verse. Since John began preaching, God’s kingdom has faced violent opposition, with powerful people trying to seize or crush it.

f.g: suffereth = endures, undergoes. The Greek can also suggest the kingdom forcefully advancing.

f.w: the violent take it by force

n: The law and the prophets pointed forward to this moment. John was the last of the old prophetic order and the bridge to the new.
John fulfilled the role of the promised Elijah who would come before the Lord — a forerunner. Latter-day revelation also calls him an Elias.

f.g: Elias = Greek form of Elijah; also a title meaning a forerunner or preparer.

n: A call to pay close attention: those willing to understand should take this truth to heart.

f.w: He that hath ears to hear

n: Jesus compares his generation to children in the marketplace who complain that others won’t play their games.

f.g: The open marketplace, where children played.

n: Some children wanted to play “wedding,” others “funeral” — but nobody would join either game. People rejected both John and Jesus.

f.g: piped = played the flute, as at a wedding.
lamented = wailed in mourning.

n: John lived austerely, fasting and avoiding wine, and critics said he was demon-possessed.
Jesus ate with all kinds of people, and critics called him a glutton and drunkard. Still, true wisdom is proven by its results.

f.g: winebibber = heavy drinker.

f.w: wisdom is justified of her children
f.g: Wisdom is shown to be right by what it produces. Some manuscripts read “by her works.”

n: Jesus rebukes the towns that saw most of his miracles yet did not change their lives.

f.g: upbraid = scold, reproach.

n: Chorazin and Bethsaida were Jewish towns near the Sea of Galilee. Even pagan Tyre and Sidon would have repented had they seen such miracles.

f.g: A town a few miles north of Capernaum; its ruins still stand.
Phoenician port cities on the Mediterranean coast, often condemned by the prophets.
Rough goat-hair clothing and ashes — outward signs of mourning and repentance.

n: Greater light brings greater accountability. Those who saw more will be judged more strictly.
Capernaum, Jesus’s own home base and honored by his presence, will be humbled for its unbelief. Even Sodom would have repented.

f.g: Greek Hades — the realm of the dead.

n: Sodom, the classic example of wickedness, will fare better in judgment than Capernaum, which saw Christ and still refused him.
Jesus thanks the Father that the truths of the kingdom are revealed to humble, childlike people rather than to the proud and self-sufficient.

f.g: Little children — the humble and teachable.
prudent = clever, worldly-wise.

n: Jesus accepts this as the Father’s good plan and wisdom.

f.w: so it seemed good in thy sight
f.g: This pleased you — it was your will.

n: The Father has entrusted all things to the Son. Only the Son truly knows the Father, and he reveals the Father to whomever he chooses.

f.w: All things are delivered unto me of my Father

f.g: save = except.

n: One of the most tender invitations in scripture. Jesus calls everyone worn out by burdens — sin, grief, rules, life — to come to him for rest.

f.g: Weighed down, like an overloaded animal.

n: A yoke joined two oxen to pull together. Jesus invites us to be yoked with him — to learn from him as he carries the load beside us.

f.g: A wooden beam fitted over the necks of draft animals; rabbis spoke of the “yoke of the law.”

n: His yoke fits well and his burden is light — not because discipleship is effortless, but because he shares the weight and gives strength.

f.g: easy = well-fitting, kind (Greek chrēstos).
